title: This Is Why You Wake Up at 3am
description: We have a new podcast studio!!! Team, you all know that I have been doing my podcast since 2016 - holy moly, it’s been 10 years!!!!!!! I have gone from recording audio only to recording on a $30 microphone in my first New York City apartment. I have gone all over the world to interview guests, and now I have my very own beautiful white studio! Go watch this one. I mean it. I sat down with Dr. Michael Breus, the Sleep Doctor, and I left rethinking things I was sure I already understood. He has spent his whole career as a clinical psychologist doing one thing, fixing the way people sleep, and he is blunt in a way I loved. First thing that floored me: the Sleep Doctor himself stops breathing 26 times an hour in his sleep, and had no idea for years. How he found out: His workouts were falling apart and his mile time kept climbing He ran bloodwork, even tried testosterone, chasing every other explanation first Nothing moved Finally someone asked when he’d last done a sleep study It came back 26. He was so sure it was broken that he retook it. Same number. The Sleep Doctor had sleep apnea and didn’t know. Here’s why that should scare the rest of us: It can happen anywhere from 5 to hundreds of times an hour, and most people never know it’s happening Every time you stop breathing, your heart rate drops then spikes to restart you, loading your heart all night long. Over time that can tip into atrial fibrillation. You’re also starving your brain of oxygen, and you never sink into the deep sleep where the brain runs its own cleanup His tell for spotting it across a room: a neck over 17.5 inches carries an 83 percent chance of apnea (his number) And one story I won’t forget: a detective, benched because he kept falling asleep on stakeouts, finally got on a CPAP.

title: New Creatine and Peri Menopause Study!!!!
description: Team!!!!! A brand new creatine study has arrived!!! And not just any creatine study. This one took perimenopausal women, gave half of them creatine and half an identical placebo, put all of them through six weeks of heavy training, and watched their brains work in real time while they did it. Creatine, in midlife women, with real brain measurements. That almost never gets studied, and this team pulled it off. You know creatine is one of the very few supplements I actually stand behind. So when a trial like this lands, I read every single line. And what they found got me fired up. Why this matters to you If you are in your forties and your brain feels like it is running too many tabs at once, this study is about you. The word that vanishes mid-sentence. The 3 a.m. wake-up. The afternoon fog that will not lift. You have been told this is just perimenopause and to wait it out. These researchers went looking for something better. What they did Fifty-one women in perimenopause, average age 46. Three groups. Most of them trained hard, twice a week, for six weeks. A smaller group did nothing, as the comparison. Half of the training women got creatine, half got placebo. And to see inside the brain, the team placed a sensor on each woman’s forehead and measured how much oxygen-rich blood her prefrontal cortex pulled in while she worked through a tough mental test. A note on sunlight, UVB, and why I’ve been using Solius This is my latest hack for circadian rhythm disruption! The obvious answer is to get outside more—and I still think that should come first. But the reality is that consistent UVB exposure is not always easy. Season, latitude, weather, work schedules, and how much time we spend indoors all change what we actually get. That’s one reason I’ve been using Solius .

title: Belly Fat Is Shrinking Your Brain
description: Team, The fat around your waist is talking to your brain. Not as a metaphor. Chemically, constantly, every single day. A major new review just sat me down and walked me through the entire conversation, from one bloated fat cell all the way up to the circuits that hold your memories. I read it twice, and on the second pass I was scribbling in the margins like a lunatic, because the story it tells about the midlife brain is one of the most important things I have read all year. Here is the scale of what we are talking about. Almost 900 million people now live with obesity, and rates of dementia are projected to nearly triple by 2050. Those two lines are converging. This review is about the exact place they meet, which is your brain. It came out in Nature Reviews Neurology. Instead of a single study, it pulls the whole field into one place, from studies of millions of people down to the precise damage happening inside individual brain cells. Let me walk you through it the way it walked me through it. Fair warning: it gets stranger as it goes. First, a paradox that broke this field for a decade For years, the data made no sense. Study after study found that being obese in old age was associated with a lower risk of dementia. Thinner older adults got dementia more often. People started calling it the “obesity paradox,” and it got used, loudly, to argue that the worry about weight and the brain was overblown. Here is the grim problem. People often start losing weight in the years before dementia is ever diagnosed. The disease is already quietly eating through the brain, appetite and behavior shift, and the number on the scale falls. So late-life thinness was never protecting anyone. It was an early symptom being mistaken for a shield.
